Tutorial

Frequency domain decomposition

Output-only modal analysis asks what a structure is doing when only its vibration is measured. This page derives frequency domain decomposition from first principles: energy, the equation of motion, eigenvalues, transfer functions, power spectra, and the singular value decomposition. It then derives enhanced FDD for damping. Every approximation is stated where it enters, together with the assumption that licenses it.

Assumptions we use

The derivation is exact under A0–A6 and A8. A7 is an estimation assumption; A9 and A10 are the FDD and EFDD approximations. Each is used where noted and revisited in §9.

Model

A0
Output-only. Only y(t)y(t)y(t) is measured; x(t)x(t)x(t) is unknown and modeled as random.
A1
Linear, time-invariant, finite-dimensional. nnn coordinates, rrr inputs, ppp sensors; small displacements about equilibrium; M,C,KM,C,KM,C,K constant.
A2
Viscous damping. Constant symmetric CCC. General damping makes the modes complex; the residue derivation still applies.
A3
Linear input and output maps. Forces enter as BxBxBx, sensors read LqLqLq; no sensor dynamics, delays, or nonlinearities.
A4
Matrix properties. M=MT≻0M=M^T\succ0M=MT≻0, K=KT⪰0K=K^T\succeq0K=KT⪰0, C=CT⪰0C=C^T\succeq0C=CT⪰0; K≻0K\succ0K≻0 if restrained. Derived from energy in §2.4.
A5
Simple, stable eigenvalues. The 2n2n2n eigenvalues are distinct, stable, and in conjugate pairs; every pole is simple. Repeated or defective roots are excluded.

Excitation and measurement

A6
Stationary random excitation. xxx is zero-mean, wide-sense stationary, with finite variance and a spectral density matrix; ergodicity lets time averages estimate ensemble averages.
A7
Accurate estimate. G^y\widehat G_yGy​ is close to GyG_yGy​; finite-record errors are treated in Appendix D.
A8
Clean, synchronized measurements. Noise is zero or uncorrelated with the response; channels are synchronized and calibrated.
A9
One dominant mode in the band. Gx(f)≈QxG_x(f)\approx Q_xGx​(f)≈Qx​, and the residual EmE_mEm​ is small relative to the selected term. Made precise in §6.
A10
One mode in the bell. The EFDD bell contains one mode and its correlation decays as a single exponential.

Conventions

A11
Fourier and spectral conventions. j2=−1j^2=-1j2=−1; Fourier transform e−j2πfte^{-j2\pi ft}e−j2πft; GyG_yGy​ two-sided unless marked +^++; one-sided spectra double interior bins but not DC or Nyquist; fff in hertz, ω=2πf\omega=2\pi fω=2πf; displacement PSD in unit2/Hz\text{unit}^2/\text{Hz}unit2/Hz.
A12
Scale and phase are not identified. The shape is fixed only up to a complex scale; modal mass is not identifiable.

The argument in one page

Each link uses only the link before it and the assumptions above.

Energy gives the equations of motion. Free vibration gives poles and mode shapes. Forcing makes each pole a rank-one residue. Random forcing makes the response PSD a sum of those rank-one terms. When one term dominates, the leading eigenvector of the PSD is the measured shape. The width of that term gives the damping.

FDD is PCA at every frequency. Gy(f)G_y(f)Gy​(f) is Hermitian positive semidefinite, so diagonalizing it is PCA on the sensor channels without centering. The first eigenvector is the dominant spatial direction; FDD identifies it with the mode shape near a resonance.

Part IThe model

1The measurement problem

Sensors record the response y(t)y(t)y(t); the forces x(t)x(t)x(t) are unknown. We want the frequencies at which the structure vibrates, the relative motion of the sensors at those frequencies, and the decay rate. A mode shape is a fixed pattern of relative amplitude and phase: with one mode, every record is a scalar multiple of one vector, so the ratio between two sensors does not change with time. With several modes the ratio varies, and the pattern is visible only in a narrow band around a resonance.

FDD estimates the cross-spectral matrix Gy(f)G_y(f)Gy​(f) and decomposes it at each frequency; the dominant direction at a peak is the shape. EFDD selects a band around a peak, inverse-transforms it, and fits the correlation decay to get damping. Because the inputs are not measured, the shape is determined only up to a complex scale; §6 shows why.

2Energy and the equation of motion

FDD relies on symmetry and positive semidefiniteness, which come from energy. We derive the equation of motion from energy and check it with Lagrange’s equations.

2.1Energy of a vibrating structure

Let q(t)∈Rnq(t)\in\mathbb R^nq(t)∈Rn collect displacements from static equilibrium. For a linear structure,

T=12q˙TMq˙,V=12qTKq,D=12q˙TCq˙.T=\tfrac12\dot q^TM\dot q,\qquad V=\tfrac12q^TKq,\qquad D=\tfrac12\dot q^TC\dot q.T=21​q˙​TMq˙​,V=21​qTKq,D=21​q˙​TCq˙​.
(2.1)

M,K,CM,K,CM,K,C are the mass, stiffness, and viscous damping matrices. External forces do virtual work

δW=(Bx)Tδq=xTBTδq,\delta W=(Bx)^T\delta q=x^TB^T\delta q,δW=(Bx)Tδq=xTBTδq,

where BBB is n×rn\times rn×r; BxBxBx is the generalized force. Sensors read

y=Lq,y=Lq,y=Lq,

with LLL of size p×np\times np×n. The quadratic forms follow from a Taylor expansion about equilibrium: the linear term vanishes at a stationary point, the constant can be taken as zero, and the quadratic term dominates for small displacements (A1). The matrices are second derivatives of the energy, hence symmetric.

2.2One degree of freedom

Take a mass μ>0\mu>0μ>0, spring k>0k>0k>0, damper b≥0b\ge0b≥0, force F(t)F(t)F(t), and displacement u(t)u(t)u(t). The energies and virtual work are

T=12μu˙2,V=12ku2,D=12bu˙2,δW=F δu.T=\tfrac12\mu\dot u^2,\qquad V=\tfrac12ku^2,\qquad D=\tfrac12b\dot u^2,\qquad \delta W=F\,\delta u.T=21​μu˙2,V=21​ku2,D=21​bu˙2,δW=Fδu.
(2.2)

Energy balance equates the rate of stored energy to the supplied power minus the dissipated power:

ddt(T+V)=Fu˙−bu˙2.\frac{d}{dt}(T+V)=F\dot u-b\dot u^2.dtd​(T+V)=Fu˙−bu˙2.
(2.3)

Differentiate and factor:

μu˙u¨+kuu˙=Fu˙−bu˙2⟹u˙(μu¨+bu˙+ku−F)=0.\mu\dot u\ddot u+ku\dot u=F\dot u-b\dot u^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\dot u\bigl(\mu\ddot u+b\dot u+ku-F\bigr)=0.μu˙u¨+kuu˙=Fu˙−bu˙2⟹u˙(μu¨+bu˙+ku−F)=0.

When u˙≠0\dot u\ne0u˙=0, divide. When u˙=0\dot u=0u˙=0, continuity of u¨\ddot uu¨ and FFF makes the bracket vanish as a limit. Hence

μu¨+bu˙+ku=F.\mu\ddot u+b\dot u+ku=F.μu¨+bu˙+ku=F.
(2.4)

Each term is a force. Dividing by μ\muμ gives the normalized form

u¨+bμu˙+kμu=Fμ.\ddot u+\frac{b}{\mu}\dot u+\frac{k}{\mu}u=\frac{F}{\mu}.u¨+μb​u˙+μk​u=μF​.

Lagrange’s equations give the same result and generalize to matrices. With Lagrangian T−VT-VT−V, dissipation DDD, and generalized force QQQ,

ddt∂(T−V)∂u˙−∂(T−V)∂u+∂D∂u˙=Q.\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial (T-V)}{\partial\dot u}-\frac{\partial (T-V)}{\partial u}+\frac{\partial D}{\partial\dot u}=Q.dtd​∂u˙∂(T−V)​−∂u∂(T−V)​+∂u˙∂D​=Q.

Here T−V=12μu˙2−12ku2T-V=\tfrac12\mu\dot u^2-\tfrac12ku^2T−V=21​μu˙2−21​ku2, D=12bu˙2D=\tfrac12b\dot u^2D=21​bu˙2, and Q=FQ=FQ=F. The derivatives are

2.3Many degrees of freedom

For the full structure, energy balance is

ddt(12q˙TMq˙+12qTKq)=q˙TBx−q˙TCq˙.\frac{d}{dt}\left(\tfrac12\dot q^TM\dot q+\tfrac12q^TKq\right)=\dot q^TBx-\dot q^TC\dot q.dtd​(21​q˙​TMq˙​+21​qTKq)=q˙​TBx−q˙​TCq˙​.

Mq¨+Cq˙+Kq=Bx,y=Lq.M\ddot q+C\dot q+Kq=Bx,\qquad y=Lq.Mq¨​+Cq˙​+Kq=Bx,y=Lq.
(2.7)

3Modal analysis: free vibration

Free vibration is the motion with no force. Its solutions are the modes: fixed spatial patterns that evolve at a single complex rate.

3.1The exponential ansatz and the quadratic eigenproblem

Set x=0x=0x=0 in (2.7):

Mq¨+Cq˙+Kq=0.M\ddot q+C\dot q+Kq=0.Mq¨​+Cq˙​+Kq=0.

This linear constant-coefficient equation has exponential solutions; polynomial factors occur only for repeated eigenvalues, excluded by A5. Seek

qc(t)=ϕeλt,q˙c=λϕeλt,q¨c=λ2ϕeλt.q_c(t)=\phi e^{\lambda t},\qquad \dot q_c=\lambda\phi e^{\lambda t},\qquad \ddot q_c=\lambda^2\phi e^{\lambda t}.qc​(t)=ϕeλt,q˙​c​=λϕeλt,q¨​c​=λ2ϕeλt.
(3.1)

Here ccc marks the complex auxiliary solution, ϕ≠0\phi\ne0ϕ=0 is the spatial pattern, and λ\lambdaλ is the complex rate. Substitution gives

(λ2M+λC+K)ϕ eλt=0.\left(\lambda^2M+\lambda C+K\right)\phi\,e^{\lambda t}=0.(λ2M+λC+K)ϕeλt=0.

Cancel the exponential and define

Z(s)=s2M+sC+K,Z(λ)ϕ=0,det⁡Z(λ)=0.Z(s)=s^2M+sC+K,\qquad Z(\lambda)\phi=0,\qquad \det Z(\lambda)=0.Z(s)=s2M+sC+K,Z(λ)ϕ=0,detZ(λ)=0.
(3.2)

Nonzero ϕ\phiϕ makes Z(λ)Z(\lambda)Z(λ) singular; a zero determinant gives a null vector. The scale of ϕ\phiϕ is arbitrary; only its direction matters. This is a quadratic eigenvalue problem. det⁡Z(s)\det Z(s)detZ(s) has degree 2n2n2n because its leading term is det⁡(M)s2n\det(M)s^{2n}det(M)s2n, so there are 2n2n2n roots, and real matrices give conjugate pairs. A numerical solver uses the 2n×2n2n\times2n2n×2n state form z=[q;q˙]z=[q;\dot q]z=[q;q˙​], whose eigenvectors stack ϕm\phi_mϕm​ on λmϕm\lambda_m\phi_mλm​ϕm​ (Appendix A).

Part IIFrom forces to spectra

4The transfer matrix and its residues

Free vibration gives the poles; the transfer matrix gives their residues. It maps forces to measurements in the frequency domain.

4.1The Laplace transform

For a signal q(t)q(t)q(t) on t≥0t\ge0t≥0,

Q(s)=L{q}(s)=∫0∞q(t)e−st dt,s=σ+jω.Q(s)=\mathcal L\{q\}(s)=\int_0^\infty q(t)e^{-st}\,dt,\qquad s=\sigma+j\omega.Q(s)=L{q}(s)=∫0∞​q(t)e−stdt,s=σ+jω.
(4.1)

This is a Fourier transform of q(t)e−σtq(t)e^{-\sigma t}q(t)e−σt; choosing σ\sigmaσ large enough makes it converge. The derivative rule follows from integration by parts with u=e−stu=e^{-st}u=e−st, dv=q˙ dtdv=\dot q\,dtdv=q˙​dt:

∫0∞q˙(t)e−st dt=[q(t)e−st]0∞+s∫0∞q(t)e−st dt=sQ(s)−q(0).\int_0^\infty\dot q(t)e^{-st}\,dt=\bigl[q(t)e^{-st}\bigr]_0^\infty+s\int_0^\infty q(t)e^{-st}\,dt=sQ(s)-q(0).∫0∞​q˙​(t)e−stdt=[q(t)e−st]0∞​+s∫0∞​q(t)e−stdt=sQ(s)−q(0).

The upper limit vanishes by the choice of σ\sigmaσ; the lower limit gives −q(0)-q(0)−q(0). Applying the rule again,

L{q˙}(s)=sQ(s)−q(0),L{q¨}(s)=s2Q(s)−sq(0)−q˙(0).\mathcal L\{\dot q\}(s)=sQ(s)-q(0),\qquad \mathcal L\{\ddot q\}(s)=s^2Q(s)-sq(0)-\dot q(0).L{q˙​}(s)=sQ(s)−q(0),L{q¨​}(s)=s2Q(s)−sq(0)−q˙​(0).
(4.2)

With zero initial conditions each derivative is multiplication by sss; the initial-condition response can be added separately. On the imaginary axis, s=jω=j2πfs=j\omega=j2\pi fs=jω=j2πf, this is the stationary frequency response.

4.2From the equation of motion to H(s)H(s)H(s)

Transform (2.7) with zero initial conditions:

(s2M+sC+K)⏟Z(s)Q(s)=BX(s),Y(s)=LQ(s).\underbrace{(s^2M+sC+K)}_{Z(s)}Q(s)=BX(s),\qquad Y(s)=LQ(s).Z(s)(s2M+sC+K)​​Q(s)=BX(s),Y(s)=LQ(s).
(4.3)

Where Z(s)Z(s)Z(s) is invertible,

Q(s)=Z(s)−1BX(s),Y(s)=LZ(s)−1BX(s),Q(s)=Z(s)^{-1}BX(s),\qquad Y(s)=LZ(s)^{-1}BX(s),Q(s)=Z(s)−1BX(s),Y(s)=LZ(s)−1BX(s),

so

Y(s)=H(s)X(s),H(s)=LZ(s)−1B.Y(s)=H(s)X(s),\qquad H(s)=LZ(s)^{-1}B.Y(s)=H(s)X(s),H(s)=LZ(s)−1B.
(4.4)

HHH is p×rp\times rp×r; HikH_{ik}Hik​ maps input kkk to sensor iii. Its entries share the denominator det⁡Z(s)\det Z(s)detZ(s). ZZZ is singular exactly at the eigenvalues, so the poles of HHH are eigenvalues unless cancelled by LLL or BBB.

4.3Partial fractions at a simple pole

For one entry with a simple pole at λm\lambda_mλm​,

Hik(s)=rik,ms−λm+gik,m(s),H_{ik}(s)=\frac{r_{ik,m}}{s-\lambda_m}+g_{ik,m}(s),Hik​(s)=s−λm​rik,m​​+gik,m​(s),

where gik,mg_{ik,m}gik,m​ is finite at λm\lambda_mλm​. This is exact. Multiply by s−λms-\lambda_ms−λm​ and take the limit:

lim⁡s→λm(s−λm)Hik(s)=lim⁡s→λm[rik,m+(s−λm)gik,m(s)]=rik,m.\lim_{s\to\lambda_m}(s-\lambda_m)H_{ik}(s)=\lim_{s\to\lambda_m}\left[r_{ik,m}+(s-\lambda_m)g_{ik,m}(s)\right]=r_{ik,m}.s→λm​lim​(s−λm​)Hik​(s)=s→λm​lim​[rik,m​+(s−λm​)gik,m​(s)]=rik,m​.

H(s)=Rms−λm+Hrest,m(s),Rm=lim⁡s→λm(s−λm)H(s).H(s)=\frac{R_m}{s-\lambda_m}+H_{\mathrm{rest},m}(s),\qquad R_m=\lim_{s\to\lambda_m}(s-\lambda_m)H(s).H(s)=s−λm​Rm​​+Hrest,m​(s),Rm​=s→λm​lim​(s−λm​)H(s).

Separate the force-to-coordinate transfer from the sensor map:

T(s)=Z(s)−1B,Q(s)=T(s)X(s),H(s)=LT(s).\mathcal T(s)=Z(s)^{-1}B,\qquad Q(s)=\mathcal T(s)X(s),\qquad H(s)=L\mathcal T(s).T(s)=Z(s)−1B,Q(s)=T(s)X(s),H(s)=LT(s).

Wm=lim⁡s→λm(s−λm)T(s).W_m=\lim_{s\to\lambda_m}(s-\lambda_m)\mathcal T(s).Wm​=s→λm​lim​(s−λm​)T(s).

Z(λm)Wm=lim⁡s→λm(s−λm)B=0.Z(\lambda_m)W_m=\lim_{s\to\lambda_m}(s-\lambda_m)B=0.Z(λm​)Wm​=s→λm​lim​(s−λm​)B=0.

Each column of WmW_mWm​ lies in the nullspace of Z(λm)Z(\lambda_m)Z(λm​), the set of vectors mapped to zero. At a simple eigenvalue that nullspace is one-dimensional, so every column is a multiple of ϕm\phi_mϕm​. If input kkk has scalar γm,k\gamma_{m,k}γm,k​,

Wm=[ϕmγm,1⋯ϕmγm,r]=ϕmγmT,γmT=[γm,1⋯γm,r].W_m=\begin{bmatrix}\phi_m\gamma_{m,1}&\cdots&\phi_m\gamma_{m,r}\end{bmatrix}=\phi_m\gamma_m^T,\qquad \gamma_m^T=\begin{bmatrix}\gamma_{m,1}&\cdots&\gamma_{m,r}\end{bmatrix}.Wm​=[ϕm​γm,1​​⋯​ϕm​γm,r​​]=ϕm​γmT​,γmT​=[γm,1​​⋯​γm,r​​].

Apply LLL, which is constant and passes through the limit:

Rm=lim⁡s→λm(s−λm)H(s)=Llim⁡s→λm(s−λm)T(s)=LWm=(Lϕm)γmT=vmγmT.R_m=\lim_{s\to\lambda_m}(s-\lambda_m)H(s)=L\lim_{s\to\lambda_m}(s-\lambda_m)\mathcal T(s)=LW_m=(L\phi_m)\gamma_m^T=v_m\gamma_m^T.Rm​=s→λm​lim​(s−λm​)H(s)=Ls→λm​lim​(s−λm​)T(s)=LWm​=(Lϕm​)γmT​=vm​γmT​.

The residue is rank one: every column is a multiple of the measured shape vmv_mvm​. If vm=0v_m=0vm​=0 the sensors do not see the mode; if γm=0\gamma_m=0γm​=0 the inputs do not excite it.

For two inputs with coefficients 222 and −3-3−3, and vm=[1,−2]Tv_m=[1,-2]^Tvm​=[1,−2]T,

Rm=[2vm−3vm]=[2−3−46]=[1−2][2−3].R_m=\begin{bmatrix}2v_m&-3v_m\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2&-3\\-4&6\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\-2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2&-3\end{bmatrix}.Rm​=[2vm​​−3vm​​]=[2−4​−36​]=[1−2​][2​−3​].

Both columns keep the ratio 1:−21:-21:−2; an input vector combines them into vm(2X1−3X2)v_m(2X_1-3X_2)vm​(2X1​−3X2​). The full HHH need not be rank one, because it contains the other modes. The rank-one statement is about one residue.

4.5The full modal sum

For real matrices the conjugate pole has residue Rˉm\bar R_mRˉm​. Summing the nnn pairs,

H(s)=∑m=1n(Rms−λm+Rˉms−λˉm),Rm=vmγmT.H(s)=\sum_{m=1}^{n}\left(\frac{R_m}{s-\lambda_m}+\frac{\bar R_m}{s-\bar\lambda_m}\right),\qquad R_m=v_m\gamma_m^T.H(s)=m=1∑n​(s−λm​Rm​​+s−λˉm​Rˉm​​),Rm​=vm​γmT​.
(4.9)

This is exact under A5, not a one-mode assumption. A zero vmv_mvm​, zero γm\gamma_mγm​, or cancellation removes a term from HHH; the mode still exists.

5The response spectral matrix

Operational forces are unknown and vary between records. We average products of Fourier coefficients, not the response itself; that average is the spectral matrix.

5.1From records to a spectral matrix

Let TTT be the record duration and y(t)y(t)y(t) the ppp-channel measurement. Define

YT(f)=∫−T/2T/2y(t)e−j2πft dt,Gy(f)=lim⁡T→∞1TE ⁣[YT(f)YT(f)H].Y_T(f)=\int_{-T/2}^{T/2}y(t)e^{-j2\pi ft}\,dt,\qquad G_y(f)=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\mathbb E\!\left[Y_T(f)Y_T(f)^H\right].YT​(f)=∫−T/2T/2​y(t)e−j2πftdt,Gy​(f)=T→∞lim​T1​E[YT​(f)YT​(f)H].
(5.1)

YTY_TYT​ is random; E\mathbb EE averages over records. The (i,k)(i,k)(i,k) entry of YTYTHY_TY_T^HYT​YTH​ is YiYˉkY_i\bar Y_kYi​Yˉk​. The factor 1/T1/T1/T converts squared transform (amplitude squared times time squared) to a density (amplitude squared per hertz). Integrating a diagonal entry over all frequencies gives that channel’s mean square, equal to its variance because the mean is zero.

The matrix is two-sided. For real signals the negative frequencies mirror the positive ones; a one-sided spectrum, marked +^++, doubles interior positive bins and keeps DC and Nyquist unchanged. The definition assumes wide-sense stationarity (A6): expected products depend only on time separation, so the limit exists. Ergodicity lets a time average estimate the ensemble average; estimation details are in Appendix D.

5.2Hermitian positive semidefiniteness

For any YYY,

(YYH)H=(YH)HYH=YYH.\left(YY^H\right)^H=\left(Y^H\right)^HY^H=YY^H.(YYH)H=(YH)HYH=YYH.

A matrix equal to its conjugate transpose is Hermitian; expectation preserves this, so GyG_yGy​ is Hermitian. Its diagonal entries are averages of ∣Yi∣2|Y_i|^2∣Yi​∣2, hence real and nonnegative. For any complex weight vector aaa, ∣aHYT∣2≥0|a^HY_T|^2\ge0∣aHYT​∣2≥0, and averaging gives

GyH=Gy,aHGya=lim⁡T→∞1TE ⁣[∣aHYT∣2]≥0.G_y^H=G_y,\qquad a^HG_ya=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\mathbb E\!\left[|a^HY_T|^2\right]\ge0.GyH​=Gy​,aHGy​a=T→∞lim​T1​E[∣aHYT​∣2]≥0.
(5.2)

So GyG_yGy​ is Hermitian positive semidefinite. The spectral theorem gives an orthonormal eigenbasis and real eigenvalues; positive semidefiniteness makes them nonnegative. With unitary UUU and diagonal Λ\LambdaΛ,

Gy=UΛUH,UHU=I,Λ=diag⁡(λ1,…,λp),λk≥0.G_y=U\Lambda U^H,\qquad U^HU=I,\qquad \Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_p),\quad \lambda_k\ge0.Gy​=UΛUH,UHU=I,Λ=diag(λ1​,…,λp​),λk​≥0.

For such a matrix the singular values are the eigenvalues and the left singular vectors are the eigenvectors. The rank is the number of nonzero eigenvalues; a rank-one matrix has one eigenvector and a one-dimensional nullspace.

5.3The input–output relation

At a fixed frequency, the stationary output transform is the transfer matrix on the imaginary axis times the input transform:

YT(f)=H(j2πf)XT(f).Y_T(f)=H(j2\pi f)X_T(f).YT​(f)=H(j2πf)XT​(f).

This is (4.4) at s=j2πfs=j2\pi fs=j2πf, for the forced part after the transient has decayed. Substitute into the outer product:

YTYTH=(HXT)(HXT)H=HXTXTHHH.Y_TY_T^H=\left(HX_T\right)\left(HX_T\right)^H=HX_TX_T^HH^H.YT​YTH​=(HXT​)(HXT​)H=HXT​XTH​HH.

At fixed frequency HHH is constant across realizations, so it passes through the expectation. Applying (5.1),

Gy(f)=H(j2πf) Gx(f) H(j2πf)H.G_y(f)=H(j2\pi f)\,G_x(f)\,H(j2\pi f)^H.Gy​(f)=H(j2πf)Gx​(f)H(j2πf)H.
(5.3)

GxG_xGx​ is r×rr\times rr×r and Hermitian positive semidefinite; GyG_yGy​ is p×pp\times pp×p. The force spectrum describes the excitation, HHH the response and the sensors.

5.4Conventions and estimation

This page defines entry (i,k)(i,k)(i,k) as YiYˉkY_i\bar Y_kYi​Yˉk​. Some software uses YˉiYk\bar Y_iY_kYˉi​Yk​, the transpose and conjugate; the estimated shape is then conjugated. Do not mix conventions. A one-sided spectrum keeps f≥0f\ge0f≥0 and doubles interior bins so that integrating over f≥0f\ge0f≥0 matches the two-sided mean square; DC and Nyquist are not doubled. The Welch estimator, its normalization, and the resolution–variance tradeoff are in Appendix D.

Part IIIFinding modes in data

6When one mode dominates

The response matrix is an exact sum of rank-one terms. FDD uses the band where one term dominates and the others are a perturbation. This section isolates that term and bounds the remainder.

6.1Isolating one pole

On the imaginary axis, s=jωs=j\omegas=jω with ω=2πf\omega=2\pi fω=2πf, separate mode mmm:

H(jω)=Rmjω−λm+Em(jω),Rm=vmγmT.H(j\omega)=\frac{R_m}{j\omega-\lambda_m}+E_m(j\omega),\qquad R_m=v_m\gamma_m^T.H(jω)=jω−λm​Rm​​+Em​(jω),Rm​=vm​γmT​.
(6.1)

EmE_mEm​ contains the conjugate pole and every other mode and is finite at ωd,m\omega_{d,m}ωd,m​ (A5). The selected denominator is

jω−λm=αm+j(ω−ωd,m),∣jω−λm∣2=αm2+(ω−ωd,m)2.j\omega-\lambda_m=\alpha_m+j(\omega-\omega_{d,m}),\qquad |j\omega-\lambda_m|^2=\alpha_m^2+(\omega-\omega_{d,m})^2.jω−λm​=αm​+j(ω−ωd,m​),∣jω−λm​∣2=αm2​+(ω−ωd,m​)2.

At ω=ωd,m\omega=\omega_{d,m}ω=ωd,m​ its magnitude is αm\alpha_mαm​, so the selected term grows like 1/αm1/\alpha_m1/αm​. The remainder has no such denominator.

6.2The exact four-term expansion

With P=Rm/(jω−λm)P=R_m/(j\omega-\lambda_m)P=Rm​/(jω−λm​) and E=EmE=E_mE=Em​, substitute into (5.3):

Gy=(P+E)Gx(P+E)H=PGxPH+PGxEH+EGxPH+EGxEH.G_y=(P+E)G_x(P+E)^H=PG_xP^H+PG_xE^H+EG_xP^H+EG_xE^H.Gy​=(P+E)Gx​(P+E)H=PGx​PH+PGx​EH+EGx​PH+EGx​EH.
(6.2)

This is exact. The first term has the selected pole twice; the middle terms mix it with the remainder; the last has the remainder twice. Since PH=RmH/(−jω−λˉm)P^H=R_m^H/(-j\omega-\bar\lambda_m)PH=RmH​/(−jω−λˉm​),

Dropping the last three terms of (6.2) is legitimate when they are small. Weight selected term and remainder by the excitation; let Gx1/2G_x^{1/2}Gx1/2​ be the PSD square root and

Pw=PGx1/2,Ew=EGx1/2.P_w=PG_x^{1/2},\qquad E_w=EG_x^{1/2}.Pw​=PGx1/2​,Ew​=EGx1/2​.

Gy=PwPwH+PwEwH+EwPwH+EwEwH.G_y=P_wP_w^H+P_wE_w^H+E_wP_w^H+E_wE_w^H.Gy​=Pw​PwH​+Pw​EwH​+Ew​PwH​+Ew​EwH​.

With ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_2∥⋅∥2​ the spectral norm, the triangle inequality and ∥AB∥2≤∥A∥2∥B∥2\|AB\|_2\le\|A\|_2\|B\|_2∥AB∥2​≤∥A∥2​∥B∥2​ give

∥Gy−PwPwH∥2≤2∥Pw∥2∥Ew∥2+∥Ew∥22.\left\|G_y-P_wP_w^H\right\|_2\le2\|P_w\|_2\|E_w\|_2+\|E_w\|_2^2.​Gy​−Pw​PwH​​2​≤2∥Pw​∥2​∥Ew​∥2​+∥Ew​∥22​.

∥Gy−PwPwH∥2≤(2ε+ε2)∥Pw∥22.\left\|G_y-P_wP_w^H\right\|_2\le(2\varepsilon+\varepsilon^2)\|P_w\|_2^2.​Gy​−Pw​PwH​​2​≤(2ε+ε2)∥Pw​∥22​.

ε\varepsilonε depends on the force spectrum, modal visibility, and pole separation, not on damping alone. A lightly damped mode can have large ε\varepsilonε near a strongly excited mode; a heavily damped mode can have small ε\varepsilonε if it is alone in the band. Appendix C repeats the bound.

6.4What the assumption really says

It does not say the structure has one mode, or that damping is small. It says that in this band the selected mode dominates the response that is actually excited and observed. A mode can be invisible because vmv_mvm​ is small (sensors near a node) or γm\gamma_mγm​ is small (forces do not excite it), even if it is lightly damped. Close modes make EEE large; colored forcing distorts the weight and can shift the peak; correlated inputs matter when several modes contribute; noise adds a full-rank term.

6.5Worked example: two sensors

Suppose one mode moves sensor 1 by 111 mm and sensor 2 by −2-2−2 mm. With a(t)a(t)a(t) the first displacement,

y(t)=[a(t)−2a(t)]=v a(t),v=[1−2].y(t)=\begin{bmatrix}a(t)\\-2a(t)\end{bmatrix}=v\,a(t),\qquad v=\begin{bmatrix}1\\-2\end{bmatrix}.y(t)=[a(t)−2a(t)​]=va(t),v=[1−2​].
(6.5)

Let A(f)A(f)A(f) be the Fourier coefficient of aaa. Linearity gives Y1=AY_1=AY1​=A, Y2=−2AY_2=-2AY2​=−2A, so

∣Y1∣2=∣A∣2,∣Y2∣2=4∣A∣2,Y1Yˉ2=−2∣A∣2.|Y_1|^2=|A|^2,\qquad |Y_2|^2=4|A|^2,\qquad Y_1\bar Y_2=-2|A|^2.∣Y1​∣2=∣A∣2,∣Y2​∣2=4∣A∣2,Y1​Yˉ2​=−2∣A∣2.

Gy(f)=Sa(f) vvT=Sa(f)[1−2−24],G_y(f)=S_a(f)\,vv^T=S_a(f)\begin{bmatrix}1&-2\\-2&4\end{bmatrix},Gy​(f)=Sa​(f)vvT=Sa​(f)[1−2​−24​],
(6.6)

where SaS_aSa​ is the PSD of aaa. For Sa>0S_a>0Sa​>0 the matrix is rank one, and

Gyv=5Sa(f) v,Gy[21]=0.G_yv=5S_a(f)\,v,\qquad G_y\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix}=0.Gy​v=5Sa​(f)v,Gy​[21​]=0.

The eigenvalue depends on excitation strength; the eigenvector gives 1:−21:-21:−2 regardless. The null vector [2,1]T[2,1]^T[2,1]T is orthogonal to vvv. The shape is defined only up to scale and phase, and where Sa=0S_a=0Sa​=0 there is no preferred direction. FDD therefore estimates shapes at peaks.

7Frequency domain decomposition

FDD diagonalizes the measured spectral matrix at each frequency. The decomposition is exact; reading the leading vector as a mode shape uses the approximation of §6.

7.1The SVD at each frequency

At frequency fif_ifi​, diagonalize the estimate G^y\widehat G_yGy​:

G^y(fi)=UiSiUiH=∑k=1psk(fi) uk(fi)uk(fi)H,s1≥s2≥⋯≥sp≥0.\widehat G_y(f_i)=U_iS_iU_i^H=\sum_{k=1}^{p}s_k(f_i)\,u_k(f_i)u_k(f_i)^H,\qquad s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots\ge s_p\ge0.Gy​(fi​)=Ui​Si​UiH​=k=1∑p​sk​(fi​)uk​(fi​)uk​(fi​)H,s1​≥s2​≥⋯≥sp​≥0.
(7.1)

The columns of UiU_iUi​ are orthonormal eigenvectors; SiS_iSi​ is diagonal. For a Hermitian positive-semidefinite matrix the SVD and eigendecomposition coincide: the singular values are the eigenvalues, and the left singular vectors are the eigenvectors. The ordering makes the first term largest.

An exact rank-one matrix has only s1≠0s_1\ne0s1​=0. The estimate is generally full rank because of other modes, noise, and finite-record errors. The question is whether s2s_2s2​ is small enough that u1u_1u1​ is close to the physical shape (Appendix E).

For G≈d vvHG\approx d\,vv^HG≈dvvH with v≠0v\ne0v=0,

(d vvH)v=d ∥v∥2 v,\left(d\,vv^H\right)v=d\,\|v\|^2\,v,(dvvH)v=d∥v∥2v,
(7.2)

so vvv is an eigenvector with eigenvalue d∥v∥2d\|v\|^2d∥v∥2. Normalizing,

u1≈ejθv∥v∥,s1≈d ∥v∥2.u_1\approx e^{j\theta}\frac{v}{\|v\|},\qquad s_1\approx d\,\|v\|^2.u1​≈ejθ∥v∥v​,s1​≈d∥v∥2.
(7.3)

The phase θ\thetaθ is arbitrary, and multiplying vvv by a constant while adjusting ddd leaves d vvHd\,vv^HdvvH unchanged. Neither phase nor scale is physical; this is why modal mass is not identifiable. For G=G0+EG=G_0+EG=G0​+E with G0=d vvHG_0=d\,vv^HG0​=dvvH, the leading vector is close to v/∥v∥v/\|v\|v/∥v∥ when ∥E∥2\|E\|_2∥E∥2​ is small relative to the spectral gap; the bound is in Appendix E. A large s1/s2s_1/s_2s1​/s2​ supports a well-defined direction; a ratio near one does not. For the two-sensor example, u1=[1,−2]T/5u_1=[1,-2]^T/\sqrt5u1​=[1,−2]T/5​ and s1=5Sas_1=5S_as1​=5Sa​.

7.3Peak frequency is not pole frequency

Even a single oscillator distinguishes the spectral peak from ωn\omega_nωn​ and ωd\omega_dωd​. With subscripts omitted, the force-to-displacement transfer function is

h(jω)=1ωn2−ω2+j2ζωnω,h(j\omega)=\frac{1}{\omega_n^2-\omega^2+j2\zeta\omega_n\omega},h(jω)=ωn2​−ω2+j2ζωn​ω1​,

∣h(jω)∣2=1(ωn2−ω2)2+4ζ2ωn2ω2.\left|h(j\omega)\right|^2=\frac{1}{(\omega_n^2-\omega^2)^2+4\zeta^2\omega_n^2\omega^2}.∣h(jω)∣2=(ωn2​−ω2)2+4ζ2ωn2​ω21​.
(7.4)

Under white forcing the displacement PSD has the same frequency dependence. Minimize the denominator D(ω)D(\omega)D(ω):

D′(ω)=2(ωn2−ω2)(−2ω)+8ζ2ωn2ω=4ω[ω2−ωn2+2ζ2ωn2].D'(\omega)=2(\omega_n^2-\omega^2)(-2\omega)+8\zeta^2\omega_n^2\omega=4\omega\left[\omega^2-\omega_n^2+2\zeta^2\omega_n^2\right].D′(ω)=2(ωn2​−ω2)(−2ω)+8ζ2ωn2​ω=4ω[ω2−ωn2​+2ζ2ωn2​].

The stationary points are ω=0\omega=0ω=0 and ω2=ωn2(1−2ζ2)\omega^2=\omega_n^2(1-2\zeta^2)ω2=ωn2​(1−2ζ2). For ζ<1/2\zeta<1/\sqrt2ζ<1/2​ the positive root is a minimum of DDD, hence a maximum of ∣h∣2|h|^2∣h∣2; for ζ≥1/2\zeta\ge1/\sqrt2ζ≥1/2​ the maximum is at ω=0\omega=0ω=0. Therefore

ωpeak=ωn1−2ζ2(ζ<1/2),ωpeak=0(ζ≥1/2).\omega_{\mathrm{peak}}=\omega_n\sqrt{1-2\zeta^2}\quad(\zeta<1/\sqrt2),\qquad \omega_{\mathrm{peak}}=0\quad(\zeta\ge1/\sqrt2).ωpeak​=ωn​1−2ζ2​(ζ<1/2​),ωpeak​=0(ζ≥1/2​).
(7.5)

For light damping the three frequencies are close; for 0<ζ<1/20<\zeta<1/\sqrt20<ζ<1/2​, ωpeak<ωd<ωn\omega_{\mathrm{peak}}<\omega_d<\omega_nωpeak​<ωd​<ωn​. Colored forcing, acceleration measurement, and finite resolution shift the observable peak; an acceleration PSD carries an extra ω4\omega^4ω4, biasing it upward.

7.4Two modes in one band

For two modes,

Gy=d1v1v1H+d2v2v2H.G_y=d_1v_1v_1^H+d_2v_2v_2^H.Gy​=d1​v1​v1H​+d2​v2​v2H​.
(7.6)

If v1Hv2=0v_1^Hv_2=0v1H​v2​=0, the eigenvectors are exactly v1,v2v_1,v_2v1​,v2​, with eigenvalues d1∥v1∥2,d2∥v2∥2d_1\|v_1\|^2,d_2\|v_2\|^2d1​∥v1​∥2,d2​∥v2​∥2. Otherwise

Gyv1=d1∥v1∥2v1+d2v2(v2Hv1),G_yv_1=d_1\|v_1\|^2v_1+d_2v_2\left(v_2^Hv_1\right),Gy​v1​=d1​∥v1​∥2v1​+d2​v2​(v2H​v1​),
(7.7)

and the second term points away from v1v_1v1​, so v1v_1v1​ is not an eigenvector. The leading vector is a mixture. What survives is the span: if d1,d2>0d_1,d_2>0d1​,d2​>0 and v1,v2v_1,v_2v1​,v2​ are independent, GyG_yGy​ maps into their two-dimensional span, and the first two singular vectors recover that span but not the individual shapes. Orthogonal measured shapes are special; they are not the same as mass-orthogonal physical modes, because LLL does not preserve the mass inner product. Equal singular values leave the basis within the subspace undetermined.

The modal assurance criterion measures agreement:

MAC⁡(u,v)=∣uHv∣2(uHu)(vHv)∈[0,1].\operatorname{MAC}(u,v)=\frac{|u^Hv|^2}{(u^Hu)(v^Hv)}\in[0,1].MAC(u,v)=(uHu)(vHv)∣uHv∣2​∈[0,1].
(7.8)

By Cauchy–Schwarz it lies in [0,1][0,1][0,1]; it is one for proportional vectors, zero for orthogonal vectors, and invariant to a common complex scale. MAC decides whether the direction at a neighboring frequency is the same mode.

7.5The algorithm

FDD, step by step

  1. Acquire. Record ppp synchronized channels with known units and orientations; choose segment length, window, and overlap.
  2. Estimate. Compute G^y(fi)\widehat G_y(f_i)Gy​(fi​) for every bin, using the same segments and window for all channel pairs and enough independent segments.
  3. Decompose. Diagonalize at each fif_ifi​ (7.1); store the singular values and leading vectors.
  4. Find peaks. Plot s1(f)s_1(f)s1​(f); a local maximum is a candidate resonance.
  5. Read the shape. At a peak take u1u_1u1​; check that s1/s2s_1/s_2s1​/s2​ is large and u1u_1u1​ is stable across bins by MAC.
  6. Estimate damping. If needed, select the bell around the peak by MAC and fit its correlation decay (§8).

Output. Damped frequency fd,mf_{d,m}fd,m​, shape u1u_1u1​ up to scale and phase, and, with EFDD, ζm\zeta_mζm​.

The eigendecomposition costs O(Nfp3)O(N_fp^3)O(Nf​p3) for NfN_fNf​ bins and ppp channels, small when ppp is small. The spectral estimate costs O(Nlog⁡N)O(N\log N)O(NlogN) per segment. In practice the hard part is sensor placement and spectral settings, not the linear algebra.

8Estimating damping: EFDD

FDD gives shape and frequency. Damping comes from the width of the spectral peak: select the part belonging to one mode, inverse-transform it, and fit the decay of its correlation.

8.1Selecting the spectral bell

Take the leading vector near a peak as the reference v^m\hat v_mv^m​. At each neighboring frequency, compute MAC⁡(uk(f),v^m)\operatorname{MAC}(u_k(f),\hat v_m)MAC(uk​(f),v^m​) and keep the bin if it exceeds a threshold; the kept set is the spectral bell. A threshold of 0.80.80.8 is a common starting point: high enough to reject a neighboring mode, low enough to keep the flanks. Track the direction by MAC, not by vector index, because the first and second singular vectors can cross. Zero the rejected bins and inspect the bell: an asymmetric or rough bell indicates contamination.

The selected spectrum is one-sided, b+(f)b^+(f)b+(f), with b+[k]b^+[k]b+[k] at kΔfk\Delta fkΔf. The +^++ scaling is defined in Appendix D: interior bins are doubled, DC and Nyquist are not.

8.2From the bell to a correlation decay

By Wiener–Khinchin, the inverse transform of the PSD is the autocorrelation. For a real even correlation the result is a cosine integral:

Rm(τ)=∫0∞b+(f)cos⁡(2πfτ) df≈Δf∑k=0N/2b+[k]cos⁡ ⁣(2πkℓN),τ=ℓfs.\mathcal R_m(\tau)=\int_0^\infty b^+(f)\cos(2\pi f\tau)\,df\approx\Delta f\sum_{k=0}^{N/2}b^+[k]\cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi k\ell}{N}\right),\qquad \tau=\frac{\ell}{f_s}.Rm​(τ)=∫0∞​b+(f)cos(2πfτ)df≈Δfk=0∑N/2​b+[k]cos(N2πkℓ​),τ=fs​ℓ​.
(8.1)

Here fsf_sfs​ is the sampling rate, NNN an even transform length, Δf=fs/N\Delta f=f_s/NΔf=fs​/N, and ℓ\ellℓ the lag index. The cosine comes from mirroring the negative frequencies. For a single mode, the correlation oscillates with envelope am(τ)=A0e−αmτa_m(\tau)=A_0e^{-\alpha_m\tau}am​(τ)=A0​e−αm​τ, A0>0A_0>0A0​>0, and period Td=2π/ωd,mT_d=2\pi/\omega_{d,m}Td​=2π/ωd,m​:

Rm(τ)∝am(τ)cos⁡(ωd,mτ),Td=2πωd,m.\mathcal R_m(\tau)\propto a_m(\tau)\cos(\omega_{d,m}\tau),\qquad T_d=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_{d,m}}.Rm​(τ)∝am​(τ)cos(ωd,m​τ),Td​=ωd,m​2π​.

8.3From log decrement to damping ratio

At two times separated by kkk periods, the envelope ratio is e−αmkTde^{-\alpha_mkT_d}e−αm​kTd​. Its logarithm per period is the logarithmic decrement:

δ=1kln⁡am(τ)am(τ+kTd)=αmTd.\delta=\frac{1}{k}\ln\frac{a_m(\tau)}{a_m(\tau+kT_d)}=\alpha_mT_d.δ=k1​lnam​(τ+kTd​)am​(τ)​=αm​Td​.
(8.2)

Substitute αm=ζmωn,m\alpha_m=\zeta_m\omega_{n,m}αm​=ζm​ωn,m​ and Td=2π/(ωn,m1−ζm2)T_d=2\pi/(\omega_{n,m}\sqrt{1-\zeta_m^2})Td​=2π/(ωn,m​1−ζm2​​); the natural frequency cancels:

δ=2πζm1−ζm2.\delta=\frac{2\pi\zeta_m}{\sqrt{1-\zeta_m^2}}.δ=1−ζm2​​2πζm​​.

Square and solve for ζm\zeta_mζm​:

δ2(1−ζm2)=4π2ζm2⟹ζm2=δ24π2+δ2⟹ζm=δ4π2+δ2,\delta^2(1-\zeta_m^2)=4\pi^2\zeta_m^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\zeta_m^2=\frac{\delta^2}{4\pi^2+\delta^2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\zeta_m=\frac{\delta}{\sqrt{4\pi^2+\delta^2}},δ2(1−ζm2​)=4π2ζm2​⟹ζm2​=4π2+δ2δ2​⟹ζm​=4π2+δ2​δ​,

taking the positive root. Then

ζm=δ4π2+δ2,fn,m=fd,m1−ζm2.\zeta_m=\frac{\delta}{\sqrt{4\pi^2+\delta^2}},\qquad f_{n,m}=\frac{f_{d,m}}{\sqrt{1-\zeta_m^2}}.ζm​=4π2+δ2​δ​,fn,m​=1−ζm2​​fd,m​​.
(8.3)

Fit several peaks: ln⁡am(τj)=ln⁡A0−αmτj\ln a_m(\tau_j)=\ln A_0-\alpha_m\tau_jlnam​(τj​)=lnA0​−αm​τj​ is a line; its slope gives αm\alpha_mαm​. Same-sign peaks are one period apart, alternating extrema half a period. Exclude the initial distorted part and the late noisy part.

8.4Practical bias

A nearby mode produces beating and biases a single-exponential fit. A bell that is too narrow truncates the peak; one that is too wide admits neighbors and noise. Leakage changes the bell shape, and nonstationary excitation changes its height. Compute the damping for several bell widths and fitting intervals. If the result moves, the bell is not isolating one mode; compare the EFDD frequency with (3.7) before reporting it.

Part IVPractice

9Using the method on measurements

The calculation is short; the checks decide whether the result means anything.

9.1Before the measurement

  • Sensor placement. A sensor at a node records none of that mode. Place sensors where the target modes are large, and use enough to distinguish the shapes; vm=Lϕmv_m=L\phi_mvm​=Lϕm​ is limited by LLL.
  • Units and directions. Record the measured quantity, units, and positive direction. Arbitrary rescaling changes the geometry seen by the SVD; apply rotations before the spectral estimate.
  • Synchronization. All channels need one time base. A constant offset adds a frequency-dependent phase shift and corrupts the cross-spectra.
  • Stationarity. The excitation must be stationary over the record or each segment; transients, gusts, and operating changes violate A6.

9.2During spectral estimation

  • Same segments and window. Use them for every entry of G^y\widehat G_yGy​; otherwise the cross-channel phase is destroyed.
  • Enough averages. One segment gives a noisy estimate with artificially low rank. Overlap adds segments but not independent averages.
  • Resolution. Segment length sets resolution; zero-padding only densifies the grid. A peak narrower than the resolution cannot be separated from its neighbor.
  • Check stability. Plot s1(f)s_1(f)s1​(f) and s1/s2s_1/s_2s1​/s2​; a peak that moves with segment length or averaging is not stable.

9.3Interpreting the decomposition

  • Stable direction. The leading vector should be stable by MAC across the peak; rapid rotation means a mixture.
  • Rank one. A large s1/s2s_1/s_2s1​/s2​ supports the interpretation; a ratio near one leaves the direction undetermined.
  • Harmonic forcing. A sinusoid also gives a narrow rank-one peak. Check whether the frequency matches a known forcing frequency and whether the shape is structural.
  • Visibility. An absent peak does not prove an absent mode; it may be weakly excited or invisible at the sensors.
  • Nonlinearity. Harmonics, combination frequencies, and amplitude-dependent shapes violate the linear model.

9.4Reporting

Report sensor coordinates and directions, measured quantity and units, shape normalization and phase convention, cross-spectrum convention, segment length, window, overlap, number of averages, and resolution. For EFDD also report the bell, MAC threshold, and fitted interval. State whether reported frequencies are damped fdf_dfd​ or natural fnf_nfn​; they differ by 1−ζ2\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}1−ζ2​. When a check fails, report the mixture or bias rather than presenting the leading vector as a mode shape.

AState-space linearization

The quadratic eigenvalue problem (3.2) can be written as an ordinary eigenproblem by including velocity in the state. Let zzz be the 2n2n2n-component state vector and III the n×nn\times nn×n identity. With zero blocks of the same size, the free equation Mq¨+Cq˙+Kq=0M\ddot q+C\dot q+Kq=0Mq¨​+Cq˙​+Kq=0 becomes

z=[qq˙],z˙=Az,A=[0I−M−1K−M−1C].z=\begin{bmatrix}q\\\dot q\end{bmatrix},\qquad \dot z=Az,\qquad A=\begin{bmatrix}0&I\\-M^{-1}K&-M^{-1}C\end{bmatrix}.z=[qq˙​​],z˙=Az,A=[0−M−1K​I−M−1C​].
(A.1)

The upper block of z˙=Az\dot z=Azz˙=Az is q˙=q˙\dot q=\dot qq˙​=q˙​, an identity. The lower block is q¨=−M−1Kq−M−1Cq˙\ddot q=-M^{-1}Kq-M^{-1}C\dot qq¨​=−M−1Kq−M−1Cq˙​, which is the free equation multiplied by M−1M^{-1}M−1. The matrix AAA is 2n×2n2n\times2n2n×2n, so it has 2n2n2n eigenvalues counted with multiplicity. They are the same eigenvalues as the quadratic problem, as the next calculation shows.

Seek a state solution z=Ψeλtz=\Psi e^{\lambda t}z=Ψeλt. Then z˙=λΨeλt\dot z=\lambda\Psi e^{\lambda t}z˙=λΨeλt, and cancelling the exponential gives AΨ=λΨA\Psi=\lambda\PsiAΨ=λΨ. Write the upper and lower nnn-component blocks of Ψ\PsiΨ as Ψ1\Psi_1Ψ1​ and Ψ2\Psi_2Ψ2​. The two block equations are

λΨ1=Ψ2,−M−1KΨ1−M−1CΨ2=λΨ2.\lambda\Psi_1=\Psi_2,\qquad -M^{-1}K\Psi_1-M^{-1}C\Psi_2=\lambda\Psi_2.λΨ1​=Ψ2​,−M−1KΨ1​−M−1CΨ2​=λΨ2​.
(A.2)

The first equation gives Ψ2=λΨ1\Psi_2=\lambda\Psi_1Ψ2​=λΨ1​. Substitute into the second and multiply by MMM:

−KΨ1−λCΨ1=λ2MΨ1⟹(λ2M+λC+K)Ψ1=0.-K\Psi_1-\lambda C\Psi_1=\lambda^2M\Psi_1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\left(\lambda^2M+\lambda C+K\right)\Psi_1=0.−KΨ1​−λCΨ1​=λ2MΨ1​⟹(λ2M+λC+K)Ψ1​=0.

Thus Ψ1\Psi_1Ψ1​ is a null vector of Z(λ)Z(\lambda)Z(λ), so it is a mode shape ϕm\phi_mϕm​, and the state eigenvector is

Ψm=[ϕmλmϕm],Z(λm)ϕm=0.\Psi_m=\begin{bmatrix}\phi_m\\\lambda_m\phi_m\end{bmatrix},\qquad Z(\lambda_m)\phi_m=0.Ψm​=[ϕm​λm​ϕm​​],Z(λm​)ϕm​=0.

Conversely, every nonzero solution of the quadratic problem produces a state eigenvector by stacking ϕm\phi_mϕm​ and λmϕm\lambda_m\phi_mλm​ϕm​. The correspondence is exact:

Z(λm)ϕm=0⟺A[ϕmλmϕm]=λm[ϕmλmϕm].Z(\lambda_m)\phi_m=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad A\begin{bmatrix}\phi_m\\\lambda_m\phi_m\end{bmatrix}=\lambda_m\begin{bmatrix}\phi_m\\\lambda_m\phi_m\end{bmatrix}.Z(λm​)ϕm​=0⟺A[ϕm​λm​ϕm​​]=λm​[ϕm​λm​ϕm​​].

In the quadratic problem, λm\lambda_mλm​ selects the matrix Z(λm)Z(\lambda_m)Z(λm​) and ϕm\phi_mϕm​ lies in its nullspace; ϕm\phi_mϕm​ does not satisfy Z(λm)ϕm=λmϕmZ(\lambda_m)\phi_m=\lambda_m\phi_mZ(λm​)ϕm​=λm​ϕm​. To recover a displacement mode shape from a state eigenvector, take its first nnn entries.

The two problems have the same 2n2n2n eigenvalues, counting repeated roots according to multiplicity. Real matrices give conjugate pairs of nonreal roots. A defective eigenvalue has fewer independent eigenvectors than its multiplicity and requires polynomial factors in time; the simple-pole expansion used in this page excludes that case. The state form also explains why the exponential ansatz is sufficient: the solution of z˙=Az\dot z=Azz˙=Az is a matrix exponential, and the matrix exponential is a combination of eλte^{\lambda t}eλt terms (with polynomial factors in the defective case).

A.1Damped modal parameters and undamped structural frequencies

There are two different meanings of “remove the damping.” For the equivalent scalar oscillator, we set its damping ratio to zero while keeping its frequency parameter ωn,m=∣λm∣\omega_{n,m}=|\lambda_m|ωn,m​=∣λm​∣. For the whole structure, we set C=0C=0C=0 in (2.7) and solve a new eigenproblem. Let Ωr\Omega_rΩr​ and ψr\psi_rψr​ denote an undamped angular frequency and its displacement shape. Substituting q=ψejΩtq=\psi e^{j\Omega t}q=ψejΩt into the undamped equation gives

Mq¨+Kq=0,Kψr=Ωr2Mψr.M\ddot q+Kq=0,\qquad K\psi_r=\Omega_r^2M\psi_r.Mq¨​+Kq=0,Kψr​=Ωr2​Mψr​.
(A.3)

This is a generalized symmetric eigenproblem. The matrix M−1KM^{-1}KM−1K is not symmetric in the ordinary inner product, but it is symmetric in the MMM-inner product, and its eigenvalues are real and nonnegative when M≻0M\succ0M≻0 and K⪰0K\succeq0K⪰0. For a single mass and spring, (A.3) and the scalar oscillator both give k/μ\sqrt{k/\mu}k/μ​.

They also agree mode by mode under proportional damping, C=aM+bKC=aM+bKC=aM+bK with constants a,ba,ba,b. To see this, apply Z(λ)Z(\lambda)Z(λ) to an undamped mode ψr\psi_rψr​ and use Kψr=Ωr2MψrK\psi_r=\Omega_r^2M\psi_rKψr​=Ωr2​Mψr​:

Z(λ)ψr=(λ2M+λaM+λbK+K)ψr=[λ2+aλ+Ωr2(1+bλ)]Mψr.Z(\lambda)\psi_r=\left(\lambda^2M+\lambda aM+\lambda bK+K\right)\psi_r=\left[\lambda^2+a\lambda+\Omega_r^2(1+b\lambda)\right]M\psi_r.Z(λ)ψr​=(λ2M+λaM+λbK+K)ψr​=[λ2+aλ+Ωr2​(1+bλ)]Mψr​.
(A.4)

Since Mψr≠0M\psi_r\ne0Mψr​=0, the bracket must vanish. It is a quadratic in λ\lambdaλ,

λ2+(a+bΩr2)λ+Ωr2=0.\lambda^2+(a+b\Omega_r^2)\lambda+\Omega_r^2=0.λ2+(a+bΩr2​)λ+Ωr2​=0.

Comparing with λ2+2ζrΩrλ+Ωr2\lambda^2+2\zeta_r\Omega_r\lambda+\Omega_r^2λ2+2ζr​Ωr​λ+Ωr2​ gives ωn,r=Ωr\omega_{n,r}=\Omega_rωn,r​=Ωr​ and ζr=(a/Ωr+bΩr)/2\zeta_r=(a/\Omega_r+b\Omega_r)/2ζr​=(a/Ωr​+bΩr​)/2. The damped mode is the undamped mode with an added decay, and the two notions of natural frequency coincide. For general damping this is not true: the damped modes can combine several undamped shapes, and ∣λm∣|\lambda_m|∣λm​∣ need not equal any Ωr\Omega_rΩr​. In this page, “natural frequency of mode mmm” always means the equivalent-oscillator parameter ωn,m=∣λm∣\omega_{n,m}=|\lambda_m|ωn,m​=∣λm​∣.

BThe residue formula via the adjugate

Section 4.4 shows that the residue is rank one, but it leaves the input-coupling vector γm\gamma_mγm​ in terms of a limit. This appendix evaluates that limit explicitly. The result is the formula used in implementations, and it shows exactly when a mode disappears from the transfer matrix.

The cofactor at row iii, column jjj of a square matrix is (−1)i+j(-1)^{i+j}(−1)i+j times the determinant after deleting row iii and column jjj. The adjugate adj⁡Z\operatorname{adj}ZadjZ is the transpose of the cofactor matrix. It remains defined at singular matrices and satisfies

Zadj⁡Z=adj⁡Z Z=(det⁡Z)I.Z\operatorname{adj}Z=\operatorname{adj}Z\,Z=(\det Z)I.ZadjZ=adjZZ=(detZ)I.
(B.1)

Wherever ZZZ is invertible, Z−1=adj⁡Z/det⁡ZZ^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}Z/\det ZZ−1=adjZ/detZ. The transfer matrix is therefore

H(s)=Ladj⁡Z(s)det⁡Z(s)B.H(s)=L\frac{\operatorname{adj}Z(s)}{\det Z(s)}B.H(s)=LdetZ(s)adjZ(s)​B.

At a simple root λm\lambda_mλm​, the determinant has a simple zero and the adjugate has rank one. The rank statement follows from (B.1): at the root, det⁡Z=0\det Z=0detZ=0, so Zadj⁡Z=0Z\operatorname{adj}Z=0ZadjZ=0. Every column of the adjugate lies in the nullspace of Z(λm)Z(\lambda_m)Z(λm​), which is one-dimensional, and the adjugate is not the zero matrix because the root is simple. Therefore

adj⁡Z(λm)=cm ϕmℓmH,\operatorname{adj}Z(\lambda_m)=c_m\,\phi_m\ell_m^H,adjZ(λm​)=cm​ϕm​ℓmH​,
(B.2)

where cm≠0c_m\ne0cm​=0 is a constant, ϕm\phi_mϕm​ is the right null vector, and ℓmH\ell_m^HℓmH​ is the left null vector, satisfying Z(λm)ϕm=0Z(\lambda_m)\phi_m=0Z(λm​)ϕm​=0 and ℓmHZ(λm)=0\ell_m^HZ(\lambda_m)=0ℓmH​Z(λm​)=0. The two null vectors are nonzero because the root is simple.

Near the root, expand the determinant in a Taylor series. Let dm′d'_mdm′​ be its derivative at λm\lambda_mλm​. Then

det⁡Z(s)=(s−λm)dm′+O ⁣((s−λm)2).\det Z(s)=(s-\lambda_m)d'_m+O\!\left((s-\lambda_m)^2\right).detZ(s)=(s−λm​)dm′​+O((s−λm​)2).
(B.3)

The symbol O((s−λm)2)O((s-\lambda_m)^2)O((s−λm​)2) denotes a remainder bounded by a constant times ∣s−λm∣2|s-\lambda_m|^2∣s−λm​∣2 near the root. The derivative is given by Jacobi’s identity, which is valid also at singular matrices:

dm′=tr⁡ ⁣(adj⁡Z(λm)Z′(λm)),Z′(s)=2sM+C.d'_m=\operatorname{tr}\!\left(\operatorname{adj}Z(\lambda_m)Z'(\lambda_m)\right),\qquad Z'(s)=2sM+C.dm′​=tr(adjZ(λm​)Z′(λm​)),Z′(s)=2sM+C.

Substituting (B.2) into the trace gives dm′=cmℓmH(2λmM+C)ϕmd'_m=c_m\ell_m^H(2\lambda_mM+C)\phi_mdm′​=cm​ℓmH​(2λm​M+C)ϕm​. Now form the residue limit. The factors s−λms-\lambda_ms−λm​ cancel, as do the constants cmc_mcm​:

Rm=lim⁡s→λm(s−λm)H(s)=Ladj⁡Z(λm)Bdm′=(Lϕm)(ℓmHB)ℓmH(2λmM+C)ϕm=vmγmT.R_m=\lim_{s\to\lambda_m}(s-\lambda_m)H(s)=\frac{L\operatorname{adj}Z(\lambda_m)B}{d'_m}=\frac{(L\phi_m)(\ell_m^HB)}{\ell_m^H(2\lambda_mM+C)\phi_m}=v_m\gamma_m^T.Rm​=s→λm​lim​(s−λm​)H(s)=dm′​LadjZ(λm​)B​=ℓmH​(2λm​M+C)ϕm​(Lϕm​)(ℓmH​B)​=vm​γmT​.
(B.4)

Thus the input-coupling vector is

γmT=ℓmHBℓmH(2λmM+C)ϕm.\gamma_m^T=\frac{\ell_m^HB}{\ell_m^H(2\lambda_mM+C)\phi_m}.γmT​=ℓmH​(2λm​M+C)ϕm​ℓmH​B​.

The denominator is nonzero at a simple root. If it were zero, the derivative of the determinant would vanish, and the root would not be simple. The residue vanishes precisely when the mode is unobserved, Lϕm=0L\phi_m=0Lϕm​=0, or unexcited, ℓmHB=0\ell_m^HB=0ℓmH​B=0. In a minimal state realization every state direction is reachable from the inputs and observable in the outputs, so no state pole is lost from the transfer matrix; individual entries can still omit modes.

For force-to-velocity and force-to-acceleration matrices, denote the transfer matrices by Hy˙H_{\dot y}Hy˙​​ and Hy¨H_{\ddot y}Hy¨​​. With zero initial conditions, differentiation becomes multiplication by sss, so Hy˙=sHH_{\dot y}=sHHy˙​​=sH. For acceleration, differentiating twice gives Hy¨=s2HH_{\ddot y}=s^2HHy¨​​=s2H. Its high-frequency limit is the feedthrough LM−1BLM^{-1}BLM−1B; equivalently, Hy¨=LM−1B+H~(s)H_{\ddot y}=LM^{-1}B+\tilde H(s)Hy¨​​=LM−1B+H~(s) with H~(s)→0\tilde H(s)\to0H~(s)→0 as s→∞s\to\inftys→∞. The residues acquire factors λm\lambda_mλm​ and λm2\lambda_m^2λm2​, and the feedthrough adds a constant term that has no pole. Real or repeated roots require a different expansion; truncating the modal sum to a few modes leaves a residual.

Inverse expansion: [1], §3.5, equation (3.11). Factorized residues: [3], equations (2)–(3). The adjugate calculation supplies the intermediate steps.

CA bound on the omitted response

This appendix repeats the bound of §6.3 with the same notation, so that the main text and the proof can be read side by side. Assume the force spectral matrix GxG_xGx​ is constant across the band and denote it by QxQ_xQx​. Let Qx1/2Q_x^{1/2}Qx1/2​ be its Hermitian positive-semidefinite square root. Define the excitation-weighted selected term and remainder

P=vmγmTjω−λm,E=Em(jω),Pw=PQx1/2,Ew=EQx1/2.P=\frac{v_m\gamma_m^T}{j\omega-\lambda_m},\qquad E=E_m(j\omega),\qquad P_w=PQ_x^{1/2},\qquad E_w=EQ_x^{1/2}.P=jω−λm​vm​γmT​​,E=Em​(jω),Pw​=PQx1/2​,Ew​=EQx1/2​.
(C.1)

Expanding (5.3) gives

Gy=PwPwH+PwEwH+EwPwH+EwEwH.G_y=P_wP_w^H+P_wE_w^H+E_wP_w^H+E_wE_w^H.Gy​=Pw​PwH​+Pw​EwH​+Ew​PwH​+Ew​EwH​.

Let ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_2∥⋅∥2​ be the matrix spectral norm. The triangle inequality and the submultiplicative property ∥AB∥2≤∥A∥2∥B∥2\|AB\|_2\le\|A\|_2\|B\|_2∥AB∥2​≤∥A∥2​∥B∥2​ give

∥Gy−PwPwH∥2≤2∥Pw∥2∥Ew∥2+∥Ew∥22.\left\|G_y-P_wP_w^H\right\|_2\le2\|P_w\|_2\|E_w\|_2+\|E_w\|_2^2.​Gy​−Pw​PwH​​2​≤2∥Pw​∥2​∥Ew​∥2​+∥Ew​∥22​.

If ∥Ew∥2≤ε∥Pw∥2\|E_w\|_2\le\varepsilon\|P_w\|_2∥Ew​∥2​≤ε∥Pw​∥2​, then

∥Gy−PwPwH∥2≤(2ε+ε2)∥Pw∥22,∥Pw∥22=∥PwPwH∥2.\left\|G_y-P_wP_w^H\right\|_2\le(2\varepsilon+\varepsilon^2)\|P_w\|_2^2,\qquad \|P_w\|_2^2=\left\|P_wP_w^H\right\|_2.​Gy​−Pw​PwH​​2​≤(2ε+ε2)∥Pw​∥22​,∥Pw​∥22​=​Pw​PwH​​2​.
(C.2)

The second equality says that the bound is relative to the size of the selected term itself, not to an unrelated scale. The number ε\varepsilonε is a sufficient condition for an accurate rank-one approximation. It is not necessary: a matrix can be close to rank one even when this particular bound is loose. What the bound makes clear is the dependence on the excitation. A small ε\varepsilonε requires the omitted response, weighted by the force spectrum, to be small compared with the selected response, also weighted by the force spectrum. Light damping alone does not produce that condition.

DSpectral conventions and estimation

The main text uses one convention for the cross-spectrum and one normalization for the spectral density. This appendix states both precisely, derives the normalization, and records the pitfalls that change a shape or a damping estimate.

D.1Conjugation order

Some sources define the cross-spectral matrix with YˉYT\bar YY^TYˉYT instead of YYHYY^HYYH. Denote that matrix by G~y\widetilde G_yGy​. Since YH=YˉTY^H=\bar Y^TYH=YˉT,

G~y=YˉYT=GyT=Gˉy.\widetilde G_y=\bar YY^T=G_y^T=\bar G_y.Gy​=YˉYT=GyT​=Gˉy​.
(D.1)

Under this convention, the rank-one term becomes G~y≈dmvˉmvmT\widetilde G_y\approx d_m\bar v_mv_m^TGy​≈dm​vˉm​vmT​. The leading vector estimates vˉm\bar v_mvˉm​, so it must be conjugated to recover the shape convention used here. Both conventions are valid; mixing them within one calculation is not. SciPy’s csd(a, b) uses conjugate-first ordering. If y[i] contains channel iii, the entry (i,j)(i,j)(i,j) of this page’s matrix is obtained with csd(y[j], y[i]). [6]

D.2Welch’s estimate

Welch’s method divides a record into possibly overlapping segments, applies the same window to every channel, and averages the spectral products. Detrending removes a fitted mean or trend. A window assigns a real weight to each sample to control the spectral spreading caused by a finite record.

Let NbN_bNb​ be the number of segments, NwN_wNw​ their length in samples, and w[ν]w[\nu]w[ν] the window at within-segment index ν\nuν. Indices bbb and kkk label segments and frequency bins. Write Yb[k]Y_b[k]Yb​[k] for the vector of unnormalized discrete Fourier transform (DFT) coefficients after detrending and windowing. A fast Fourier transform (FFT) computes the DFT efficiently. The one-sided factor ηk\eta_kηk​ is 222 at interior positive-frequency bins and 111 at DC and Nyquist, when present. At sampling rate fsf_sfs​, the estimate is

G^y+[k]=ηkNbfs∑ν=0Nw−1w[ν]2∑b=1NbYb[k]Yb[k]H.\widehat G_y^+[k]=\frac{\eta_k}{N_b f_s\sum_{\nu=0}^{N_w-1}w[\nu]^2}\sum_{b=1}^{N_b}Y_b[k]Y_b[k]^H.Gy+​[k]=Nb​fs​∑ν=0Nw​−1​w[ν]2ηk​​b=1∑Nb​​Yb​[k]Yb​[k]H.
(D.2)

The normalization is easiest to check on white noise. Suppose a channel is white with variance σ2\sigma^2σ2 and sampling rate fsf_sfs​. Its two-sided PSD is constant, G=σ2/fsG=\sigma^2/f_sG=σ2/fs​, because integrating a constant over the Nyquist band [−fs/2,fs/2][-f_s/2,f_s/2][−fs​/2,fs​/2] gives Gfs=σ2Gf_s=\sigma^2Gfs​=σ2. For one segment, the expected squared magnitude of the windowed DFT coefficient is E∣Yb[k]∣2=σ2∑νw[ν]2\mathbb E|Y_b[k]|^2=\sigma^2\sum_\nu w[\nu]^2E∣Yb​[k]∣2=σ2∑ν​w[ν]2. Substituting G=σ2/fsG=\sigma^2/f_sG=σ2/fs​ gives

E∣Yb[k]∣2=G fs∑ν=0Nw−1w[ν]2.\mathbb E|Y_b[k]|^2=G\,f_s\sum_{\nu=0}^{N_w-1}w[\nu]^2.E∣Yb​[k]∣2=Gfs​ν=0∑Nw​−1​w[ν]2.

Dividing by fs∑w2f_s\sum w^2fs​∑w2 therefore gives an unbiased estimate of GGG, and averaging over NbN_bNb​ segments reduces its variance. The factor ηk\eta_kηk​ converts the two-sided density to the one-sided convention. For a colored signal the window convolves the spectrum, so the estimate is a smoothed version of the true density; the normalization preserves the integral, not the exact shape.

Using identical segments and windows preserves the Hermitian positive-semidefinite structure. Each segment contributes at most one independent direction to the average, so the estimated rank cannot exceed NbN_bNb​. This is a finite-data rank, not a physical one. Averaging reduces variability between estimates, but it does not eliminate a persistent noise or forcing spectrum. Longer segments improve frequency resolution; more effectively independent segments improve averaging. Overlap does not make segments independent. Appending zeros before the DFT only samples the same windowed spectrum more densely; it does not improve the resolution set by the segment duration and window. [5]

D.3Density units and the inverse transform

The spectra here are densities per hertz. With superscripts (f)(f)(f) and (ω)(\omega)(ω) labeling density per hertz and per radian per second, the change of variables dω=2π dfd\omega=2\pi\,dfdω=2πdf gives

G(ω)(ω)=12πG(f) ⁣(ω2π).G^{(\omega)}(\omega)=\frac{1}{2\pi}G^{(f)}\!\left(\frac{\omega}{2\pi}\right).G(ω)(ω)=2π1​G(f)(2πω​).
(D.3)

For the EFDD inverse transform, the one-sided spectrum must be mirrored to negative frequencies before the inverse DFT. Halve the one-sided interior positive bins, copy them to the corresponding negative bins, and keep the DC and Nyquist endpoint weights from (D.2). With the inverse DFT normalization 1/N1/N1/N, the correlation is fsf_sfs​ times the inverse DFT of the mirrored spectrum, because the frequency spacing is Δf=fs/N\Delta f=f_s/NΔf=fs​/N and the inverse transform sums Δf G[k]ej2πkℓ/N\Delta f\,G[k]e^{j2\pi k\ell/N}ΔfG[k]ej2πkℓ/N. Normalizing by Rm(0)\mathcal R_m(0)Rm​(0) removes an overall scale but does not repair incorrect mirroring or incorrect endpoint weights. An incorrect one-sided scaling is a common cause of a biased damping estimate. [5]

D.4Additive sensor noise

Let η(t)\eta(t)η(t) denote sensor noise and GηG_\etaGη​ its PSD. If the noise and structural response have zero cross-covariance at every lag, their spectra add:

Gy+η=Gy+Gη.G_{y+\eta}=G_y+G_\eta.Gy+η​=Gy​+Gη​.
(D.4)

Correlated noise introduces additional cross terms. A large singular value can therefore reflect the measurement process as well as the structure. Noise raises all singular values, but it affects the smaller ones proportionally more, so it reduces the ratio s1/s2s_1/s_2s1​/s2​ that the rank-one interpretation relies on.

EA perturbation bound for the leading singular vector

Section 7.2 claims that the leading singular vector is close to the physical shape when the perturbation is small. This appendix makes that statement precise. The argument is short and gives the main dependence; a sharper version with the spectral gap is the Davis–Kahan theorem. [11]

Let G=G0+EG=G_0+EG=G0​+E be Hermitian, with G0=d vvHG_0=d\,vv^HG0​=dvvH, ∥v∥=1\|v\|=1∥v∥=1, and d>0d>0d>0. Let uuu be a unit eigenvector of GGG for its largest eigenvalue λ1\lambda_1λ1​, and assume λ1>0\lambda_1>0λ1​>0. Decompose uuu into a component along vvv and a component orthogonal to it:

u=αv+βw,w⊥v,∥w∥=1,∣α∣2+∣β∣2=1.u=\alpha v+\beta w,\qquad w\perp v,\qquad \|w\|=1,\qquad |\alpha|^2+|\beta|^2=1.u=αv+βw,w⊥v,∥w∥=1,∣α∣2+∣β∣2=1.

The angle θ\thetaθ between uuu and vvv satisfies sin⁡θ=∣β∣\sin\theta=|\beta|sinθ=∣β∣. Because uuu is an eigenvector, Gu=λ1uGu=\lambda_1uGu=λ1​u. Take the inner product with www:

λ1β=wHGu=wH(G0+E)u.\lambda_1\beta=w^HGu=w^H(G_0+E)u.λ1​β=wHGu=wH(G0​+E)u.

The unperturbed term vanishes: wHG0u=d wHv(vHu)=0w^HG_0u=d\,w^Hv(v^Hu)=0wHG0​u=dwHv(vHu)=0, because w⊥vw\perp vw⊥v. Therefore λ1β=wHEu\lambda_1\beta=w^HEuλ1​β=wHEu, and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives

∣β∣≤∥E∥2λ1,sin⁡θ≤∥E∥2λ1.|\beta|\le\frac{\|E\|_2}{\lambda_1},\qquad \sin\theta\le\frac{\|E\|_2}{\lambda_1}.∣β∣≤λ1​∥E∥2​​,sinθ≤λ1​∥E∥2​​.
(E.1)

This is the basic bound. It says that the angular error is controlled by the perturbation relative to the leading eigenvalue. Since λ1\lambda_1λ1​ is approximately ddd, and s1s_1s1​ estimates λ1\lambda_1λ1​, a large s1s_1s1​ relative to the perturbation is favourable.

A sharper form replaces λ1\lambda_1λ1​ by the gap between the first and second eigenvalues. If the leading eigenvalue is simple and the perturbation does not close the gap, the Davis–Kahan theorem gives

sin⁡θ≤∥E∥2λ1−λ2.\sin\theta\le\frac{\|E\|_2}{\lambda_1-\lambda_2}.sinθ≤λ1​−λ2​∥E∥2​​.

When the second eigenvalue is close to the first, the denominator is small and the bound is weak, which is the quantitative version of the statement that a ratio s1/s2s_1/s_2s1​/s2​ near one leaves the direction undetermined. When the gap is large, the direction is stable even if the absolute perturbation is not tiny. The bound is sufficient, not necessary: a direction can be stable for reasons this inequality does not capture.

Quadratic eigenproblem (3.1)–(3.2), state form (A.1)–(A.4)[1], introduction and §§3.4–3.6. Substitution, block calculation, and the proportional-damping reduction shown here.
Pole parameters (3.7), free response (3.8)[9], §2, for the scalar oscillator; [3], §2, for modal parameters. Coefficient matching and initial-condition solutions shown here.
Laplace transform (4.1)–(4.2), transfer matrix (4.4)[10] for the transform; [2] for transfer functions and minimal realizations. Integration by parts and the matrix inversion shown here.
Residues (4.5)–(4.9), adjugate proof (B.1)–(B.4)[1], §3.5; [3], equations (2)–(3). The adjugate calculation supplies the intermediate steps.
PSD (5.1)–(5.3), Welch estimate (D.2)[5] and [6]. Matrix positivity, normalization, and the one-sided scaling worked out here.
Rank-one approximation (6.1)–(6.4), residual bound (C.1)–(C.2)[3], §§2–3. The four-term expansion and the norm bound are derived here.
FDD (7.1)–(7.8), perturbation bound (E.1)[3], §3; [4], close-mode examples; [11] for the gap form. Eigenpair, peak location, and two-mode calculations derived here.
EFDD (8.1)–(8.3)[4], p. 699; [7]. Correlation scaling and decrement algebra shown here; leakage discussed in [8].

References

  1. Tisseur, F. & Meerbergen, K. (2001). The Quadratic Eigenvalue Problem. SIAM Review, 43(2), 235–286. DOI.University repository full text. §§3.4–3.6 cover linearization, the inverse and repeated/defective eigenvalues.
  2. Åström, K. J. & Murray, R. M. Feedback Systems — Transfer Functions. Author-hosted chapter draft, 22 October 2016.Transfer-function/state-space relationship and the reachable/observable part of the Kalman decomposition; see also exercise 9.8.
  3. Brincker, R., Zhang, L. & Andersen, P. (2000). Output-Only Modal Analysis by Frequency Domain Decomposition. Proceedings of ISMA25, vol. 2, 717–723.Full-text conference source used for the equation references here. Related journal article: Modal identification of output-only systems using frequency domain decomposition, Smart Materials and Structures 10 (2001), 441–445.
  4. Brincker, R., Ventura, C. E. & Andersen, P. (2001). Damping Estimation by Frequency Domain Decomposition. Proceedings of IMAC XIX, 698–703.Bell tracking, correlation decay, extrema regression, and examples with close modes, nonorthogonal shapes and correlated input.
  5. SciPy documentation. Signal Processing — Spectral Analysis.Fourier normalization, spectral densities, windowing and the resolution/variance tradeoff.
  6. SciPy documentation. scipy.signal.csd.See Notes for conjugate-first cross spectra and window scaling; cites Welch’s original 1967 paper.
  7. Structural Vibration Solutions. ARTeMIS Modal Help — Enhanced Frequency Domain Decomposition.Implementation guidance: branch matching, a starting MAC threshold of 0.8, and choosing a valid regression interval.
  8. Zhang, L., Tamura, Y., Yoshida, A., Cho, K., Nakata, S. & Naito, S. (2002). Ambient Vibration Testing & Modal Identification of an Office Building. Proceedings of IMAC XX.See the damping-estimation discussion and Table 2/Figure 9 for the influence of PSD resolution and leakage.
  9. MIT OpenCourseWare (2017). Damped Oscillations. Lecture 4, Introduction to Oscillations and Waves.§2 derives the scalar oscillator equation, exponential roots, and damping regimes. The damping ratio here is the notes’ decay parameter divided by the undamped angular frequency.
  10. MIT OpenCourseWare (2018). Topic 12: Laplace Transform. Complex Variables with Applications.Transform definition, convergence, and the derivative rule obtained by integration by parts.
  11. Davis, C. & Kahan, W. M. (1970). The rotation of eigenvectors by a perturbation. III. SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis, 7(1), 1–46.Eigenvector perturbation bounds. The gap form used in Appendix E is the sin θ theorem.

All explanatory figures on this page are computed specifically for this tutorial; no paper figures are reproduced.
